title: Proverbs 8:1–11
context: In contrast to the woman of chapter 7, who lurks in the dark, Wisdom calls aloud in public places: the heights, the crossroads, the city gates. She addresses all people, including the simple and fools, and promises words that are right, true, and plain to those who understand. Her instruction is worth more than silver, gold, or rubies.

verses.text: Doesn’t wisdom cry out? Doesn’t understanding raise her voice?
verses.arminianNotes: Doesn’t wisdom cry out? In contrast to folly’s whisper in the dark, wisdom calls openly. Arminian readers see God’s wisdom freely offered to all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see wisdom’s public proclamation, which they relate to God’s general revelation and the preached word calling all who hear.

verses.text: On the top of high places by the way, where the paths meet, she stands.
verses.arminianNotes: She stands on the heights and at the crossroads. Arminian readers note that wisdom goes where people are making decisions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the openness of wisdom’s call: no one can claim it was hidden. Wisdom stands at the places where travelers must decide which way to go.

verses.text: Beside the gates, at the entry of the city, at the entry doors, she cries aloud:
verses.arminianNotes: At the gates and city entrances she cries aloud. Arminian readers see the gates, places of commerce and justice, as the arena where wisdom shapes public life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wisdom claiming every sphere of life, including law, trade, and government. The gate was where elders judged cases, so wisdom’s voice is heard where public decisions are made.

verses.text: “I call to you men! I send my voice to the sons of mankind.
verses.arminianNotes: I call to you men; I send my voice to the sons of mankind. Arminian readers see a universal call: wisdom addresses all humanity, not a select group.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also affirm the universal offer of wisdom’s call. Many distinguish this outward call to all from the inward, effectual call by which God draws his elect.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm wisdom’s call goes to all people. Arminian readers typically see it as a sincere invitation all can answer by enabling grace. Reformed readers typically see it as a sincere outward call accompanied, for the elect, by God’s effectual inward call.

verses.text: You simple, understand prudence! You fools, be of an understanding heart!
verses.arminianNotes: You simple, understand prudence; you fools, be of an understanding heart. Arminian readers see hope for the simple: they can learn, and wisdom invites them to.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the call to the simple as an expression of God’s goodness. The command to understand is answered where God gives understanding, as 2:6 says.

verses.text: Hear, for I will speak excellent things. The opening of my lips is for right things.
verses.arminianNotes: Hear, for I will speak excellent things. Arminian readers stress that wisdom’s words are noble and right, worthy of trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm the excellence and rightness of wisdom’s speech, which reflects God’s own truthfulness.

verses.text: For my mouth speaks truth. Wickedness is an abomination to my lips.
verses.arminianNotes: My mouth speaks truth; wickedness is an abomination to my lips. Arminian readers see wisdom’s moral character as inseparable from truth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wisdom sharing God’s moral perfection, in contrast to the seductress’s deceit. Her truthfulness makes her a trustworthy guide, where folly’s smooth words lead to death.

verses.text: All the words of my mouth are in righteousness. There is nothing crooked or perverse in them.
verses.arminianNotes: All my words are in righteousness; nothing crooked or perverse. Arminian readers note the contrast with the flattering speech of 7:21.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note wisdom’s straightness, a mark of God’s word, as Psalm 19:8 says. Because her words are straight, the one who follows them is not led into crooked paths.

verses.text: They are all plain to him who understands, right to those who find knowledge.
verses.arminianNotes: They are plain to him who understands. Arminian readers stress clarity: wisdom is accessible to the willing and humble. Nothing in wisdom’s speech is hidden from the humble learner.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that understanding is itself a condition for seeing wisdom’s plainness, and that understanding comes from God.

verses.text: Receive my instruction rather than silver, knowledge rather than choice gold.
verses.arminianNotes: Receive my instruction rather than silver. Arminian readers see a call to choose values rightly. Choosing instruction over silver means letting wisdom set the priorities of life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wisdom’s worth surpassing material wealth, as in Psalm 19:10. The comparison does not despise wealth but ranks it below the knowledge of God’s ways.

verses.text: For wisdom is better than rubies. All the things that may be desired can’t be compared to it.
verses.arminianNotes: Wisdom is better than rubies; nothing desired compares. Arminian readers see the supreme value of wisdom, worth pursuing above all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the echo of 3:15. Many relate wisdom’s supreme worth to Christ, in whom are hidden all treasures of wisdom, as Colossians 2:3 says.
